# Education in Australia
Education in Australia is regulated primarily by state and territory governments, with the federal government providing funding support to non-government schools and public universities, as well as administering a national student loan scheme (HECS). Compulsory education laws vary by jurisdiction but generally require school attendance from ages five to six through fifteen to seventeen. Early childhood education, though not mandatory, is widely supported, with preschools guided by a national Early Years Learning Framework introduced in 2009.
The majority of school students (about 64%) attend government (public) schools, with the remainder in Catholic and independent (private) schools. Government schools are mostly free but may request voluntary fees, while non-government schools charge tuition supplemented by government funding. School years typically run from late January/early February to December. The Australian Curriculum, developed progressively since 2010, sets national standards across subjects for primary to senior secondary education.
Secondary education often covers Years 7 to 12, with options for specialized or selective schools based on academic merit. Australia also has special schools catering to students with disabilities, and a range of specialist and international schools. Student performance assessments include national standardized tests such as NAPLAN, complemented by international evaluations like PISA.
Tertiary education encompasses 42 universities (mostly public), vocational education and training (TAFE), and other accredited institutions. Australia is notable for its large international student population, representing a significant economic and demographic factor. Funding reforms and initiatives such as the Gonski reports have aimed to address school funding equity. The education system also prioritizes closing gaps for Indigenous Australians, with targets to increase attendance and attainment. Religious education varies by state, with some government schools offering approved special religious instruction. Issues such as school violence and debates over funding continue to be areas of focus.
